¶
'''blasty''' (blȧs′ti), ''a.'' [< ''blast'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Stormy; gusty: as, a ''blasty'' day. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.]—'''2.''' Causing a blast or blight upon vegetation: as, “a ''blasty'' noon,” ''Boyle'', Works, III. 154.

'''blatancy''' (blā′ta̤n-si), ''n.'' [< ''blatant'': see ''-ancy''.] Blatant quality.

'''blatant''' (blā′tant), ''a.'' [Also written ''blattant''; one of Spenser’s words, in ''blatant beast'', perhaps a mere alliterative invention; otherwise intended for *''blatand'', Sc. ''blaitand'', archaic ppr. of ''blate''<sup>3</sup>, var. of ''bleat''.] Bellowing; bawling; noisy; loud-talking or loud-sounding.
{{smaller block|Glory, that ''blatant'' word, which haunts some military minds like the bray of the trumpet.
{{right|''Irving.''}}}}
{{smaller|'''Blatant''' (or '''blattant''') '''beast''', calumny; scandal: symbolized by Spenser as a dreadful fiend, with a thousand tongues, begotten of Cerberus and Chimæra. ''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. i. 7.}}
{{smaller block|The Isle of Dogges where the ''blatant beast'' doth rule and raigne.
{{right|''Return from Parnassus'' (1606), v. 4.}}}}

'''blatantly''' (blā′ta̤nt-li), ''adv.'' In a blatant manner.

'''blatch†''', ''n.'' [< ME. ''blacche'', appar. < AS. *''blæcce'' (not found), < ''blæc'', black: see ''black'', and cf. ''bletch''.] Blacking.

'''blatch†''', ''v. t.'' [< ME. *''blacchen'', ''blæcchen''; from the noun. Cf. ''black'', ''v.'', and ''bletch'', ''v.'' Not connected with ''blotch'', q. v.] To smear with blacking; black.
{{smaller block|No man can like to be smutted and ''blatched'' in his face.
{{right|''Harmar'', tr. of Beza’s Sermons, p. 195.}}}}

'''blate<sup>1</sup>''' (blāt), ''a.'' [Formerly also written ''blait'', ''bleat''; appar. < ME. (Sc.) ''blate'', < AS. ''blāt'', pale, ghastly; cf. OHG. ''bleizza'', lividness.]
readings.c1s2:
{{smaller|'''1†.''' Pale; ghastly.—'''2†.''' Dull; spiritless; stupid.—'''3†.''' Blunt; curt.—'''4.''' Bashful; diffident. [North. Eng. and Scotch.]}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The youngster’s artless heart o’erflows wi’ joy,
But ''blate'' and laithfu’, scarce can weel behave.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Cottar’s Saturday Night.}}
<poem>Says Lord Mark Car, “Ye are na ''blate''
To bring us the news o’ your ain defeat—
Get out o’ my sight this morning.”</poem>
{{right|''Jacobite Ballad'', Johnnie Cope.}}}}
'''blate<sup>2</sup>''' (blāt), ''a.'' [Also written ''blait''; appar. < ME. ''blete'', naked, bare, < AS. ''bleát'', miserable (naked?), = OFries. ''blāt'', NFries. ''bleat'', naked, miserable, = MD. ''blōt'', D. ''bloot'', naked, bare, = MLG. ''blōt'', naked, bare, miserable, mere, = OHG. MHG. ''blōz'', G. ''bloss'', naked, bare, mere. Cf. ''blot''<sup>2</sup>.] Naked; bare. [Scotch.]

'''blate<sup>3</sup>''' (blāt), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''blated'', ppr. ''blating''. [Appar. a dial. var. of ''bleat'' (formerly pron. as ''blate''). Cf. ''blatant''.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To babble; prate.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To babble or prate about.
{{smaller block|He ''blates'' to me what has passed between other people and him. {{right|''Pepys'', Diary (ed. 1879), IV. 46.}}}}
'''blaterate†''', ''v. i.'' [< L. ''blateratus'', pp. of ''blaterare'', babble. Cf. ''blatter''.] To babble.

'''blateration''' (blat-ẹ-rā′sho̤n), ''n.'' [< LL. ''blateratio(n-)'', < L. ''blaterare'', babble: see ''blaterate''.] Senseless babble. [Rare.]

'''blather''' (blaᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''v. i.'' [Sc. also ''blether'', = Icel. ''bladhra'', talk inarticulately, talk nonsense (''bladhr'', nonsense), = G. dial. ''bladdern'', talk nonsense; partly imitative, and the same as ''blat-''
readings.c1s3:
''ter'', q. v.] To talk nonsense.

'''blather''' (bläᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''n.'' [Sc. also ''blether''; cf. Icel. ''bladhr'', nonsense; from the verb.] '''1.''' Nonsense; foolish talk.—'''2.''' A person who talks nonsense.

'''blatherskite''' (blaᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-skīt), ''n.'' [Also in Sc. ''bletherskite'', ''bletherskate''; < ''blather'', ''blether'', + ''skate'', a term of contempt.] '''1.''' One who talks nonsense in a blustering way; a blusterer. Hence—'''2.''' A good-for-nothing fellow; a “beat.” [Scotch and Amer.]

'''blathery''' (blaᴛ̵ʜ′ẹ-ri), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Sc., < ''blather'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Unsubstantial; trashy.

'''II.''' ''n.'' That which is unsubstantial, trashy, or deceptive.

'''Blatta'''<sup>1</sup> (blat′ä), ''n.'' [L., an insect that shuns the light, a cockroach, etc.] '''1.''' The typical genus of the family ''Blattidæ'': formerly coextensive with the family, but now greatly restricted. {{smaller|Thus, the cockroach or common black-beetle, introduced from the East into Europe and America, is ''Blatta'' (''Periplaneta'') ''orientalis''. See cut under ''Blattidæ''.}}

'''2.''' [''l. c.''] A member of this genus.

'''blatta'''<sup>2</sup> (blat′ä), ''n.'' [ML.] A purple silk interwoven with gold, used in the early middle ages. ''Rock'', Textile Fabrics.

'''blatteant†''' (blat′ē-an), ''a.'' [< ''blatta''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ean''.] Purple; of a purple color.

'''blatter''' (blat′ėr), ''v. i.'' [= G. dial. ''blattern'', ''bladdern'', prate; cf. L. ''blaterare'', ''blacterare'', talk nonsense, ''blatire'', babble (cf. ''blaterate''); cf. ''blather'', ''blate''<sup>3</sup>, ''bleat'', ''blab'', ''blabber'', ''babble'', ''brab-''
readings.c2s2:
{{smaller|omnivorous. When numerous they cause much annoyance and injury, as in bakeries, granaries, etc. See also cut under ''Insecta''.}}

'''blattiform''' (blat′i-fôrm), ''a.'' [< L. ''blatta'', a cockroach, + ''forma'', form.] Having the form of a blatta or cockroach.

'''Blattina''' (bla-tī′nä̤), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Blatta''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ina''<sup>2</sup>.] A group of cursorial orthopterous insects, including only the family ''Blattidæ'': same as ''Cursoria'', 2.

'''blattoid''' (blat′oid), ''a.'' [< ''Blatta''<sup>1</sup> + ''-oid''.] Pertaining to or having the characteristics of the ''Blattidæ''; like a cockroach.

'''blaubok''', ''n.'' See ''blauwbok''.

'''blaud''' (blâd), ''n.'' [Sc., also ''blad'', perhaps same as ''blade'' (see ''blad''<sup>3</sup> and ''blade''); but cf. Gael. ''bladh'' = Ir. ''bladh'', a part.] '''1.''' A large piece of anything; a considerable portion; a flat piece of anything.—'''2.''' A slap; a blow or stroke.

'''blaufish''' (blâ′fish), ''n.'' [< *''blau'', prob. same as Sc. ''bla'', ''blae'', dark, livid (see ''blae''), + ''fish''.] According to Pennant, a name of the blackfish, ''Centrolophus pompilus''. See cut under ''Centrolophus''.

'''blaunch†''', ''a.'' An obsolete form of ''blanch''<sup>1</sup>.

'''blauwbok''' (blou′bok), ''n.'' [D., lit. blue buck, < ''blauw'' (''blaauw''), = E. ''blue'', + ''bok'' = E. ''buck''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' The Dutch colonial name of a South African antelope, ''Hippotragus'' (or ''Ægoceros'') ''leucophæus'', given on account of its bluish appearance, caused by the dark hide showing through light hair. {{smaller|It is related to the oryx, addax, etc., and has rather large horns curving backward. Also called ''blue-''}}

''{{smaller|buck, blue antelope,}}'' {{smaller|and}} ''{{smaller|etaac.}}''

'''2.''' A small South African antelope with very short straight horns and heavy hind quarters.

Also spelled ''blaubok.''

'''blaver, blavert''' (blā′vėr, -vėrt), ''n.'' Corrupt forms of ''blawort.'' [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Your gloves shall be o’ the green clover
Come lockerin’ to your hand,
Well dropper o’er wi’ blue ''blavers,''
That grow amang white land.</poem>
{{right|''Gardener Lad'' (Anon.).}}}}

'''blaw''' (blâ), ''v.''; pret. ''blew,'' pp. ''blawn,'' ppr. ''blawing.'' [Sc., = E. ''blow''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To blow; breathe; publish; brag; boast; magnify in narrative.—{{smaller|'''To blaw in one’s lug,''' to cajole; flatter a person. Hence, ''blaw-in-my-lug,'' a flatterer; a wheedler. Scott.}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To flatter; coax.

''blather'', ''blate''<sup>3</sup>, ''bleat'', ''blab'', ''blabber'', ''babble'', ''brabble, prattle'', etc., all more or less imitative.]   '''1.''' To give forth or produce a quick succession of slight sounds; patter: as, “the rain ''blattered,''” ''Jeffrey.''—'''2.''' To speak or prate volubly; rail or rage. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|However envy list to ''blatter'' against him.
{{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}} {{img float|file=century v01 p0607 c2f1.png|width=137px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Anatomy of the Cockroach (''Blatta'' (''Periplaneta'') ''orientalis'').—Female, in longitudinal section. ''I''-''XX'', somites of the body; 1-11, abdominal somites; ''A'', antenna; ''H'', position of heart; ''N'', thoracic ganglia; ''a'', mouth; ''b'', esophagus; ''c'', ingluvies or crop; ''d'', proventriculus; ''e'', pyloric cæca; ''f'', chylific ventricle; ''g'', insertion of Malpighian cæca; ''h'', intestine; ''i'', rectum; ''k'', salivary receptacle; ''l'', salivary gland; ''lb'', labrum; ''m'', cerebral ganglia; ''v'', vulva; ''x'', cerci.}}}}

'''blatter''' (blat′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''blatter, v.'']   '''1.''' A rattling or clattering noise (as of boards falling).—'''2.''' A volley of clattering words.

'''blatterer''' (blat′ėr-ėr), ''n.'' One who blatters; a noisy blustering boaster.

'''blattering''' (blat′ėr-ing), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''blatter, v.'']   Senseless blustering.

'''blatteroon†''' (blat-ẹ-rön′), ''n.''   [< L. ''blatero(n-)'', a babbler, < ''blaterare'', babble: see ''blatter.'']   A senseless babbler.
{{smaller block|I trusted T. P. with a weighty secret, conjuring him that it should not take air and go abroad, . . . but it went out of him the very next day. . . . I hate such ''blatteroons.''
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, ii. 75.}}}}

'''Blattidæ''' (blat′i-dē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Blatta''<sup>1</sup> + ''-idæ.'']   A family of cursorial orthopterous insects, the cockroaches, coextensive with the division ''Blattina'' or suborder ''Cursoria'', or even the order ''Dictyoptera.'' {{smaller|They have a flattened, lengthened, ovate body, with head retracted into the large shield-like prothorax; long, filamentous, many-jointed antennæ; long, strong cursorial legs, with setose tibiæ; 5-jointed tarsi, with an accessory joint or plantula between the claws; large coriaceous fore wings which overlap, and longitudinal folded hind wings, both sometimes undeveloped in females. The genera, species, and individuals are numerous, and are found in all parts of the world. Some attain a very large size in the tropics. They are mostly nocturnal, or live in dark places, and most of them are omnivorous. When numerous they cause much annoyance and injury, as in bakeries, granaries, etc. See also cut under ''Insecta''.}}

'''blattiform''' (blat′i-fôrm), ''a.''   [< L. ''blatta'', a cockroach, + ''forma'', form.]   Having the form of a blatta or cockroach.

'''Blattina''' (bla-tī′nä̤), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Blatta''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ina''<sup>2</sup>.]   A group of cursorial orthopterous insects, including only the family ''Blattidæ'': same as ''Cursoria'', 2.

'''blattoid''' (blat′oid), ''a.''   [< ''Blatta''<sup>1</sup> + ''-oid''.]   Pertaining to or having the characteristics of the ''Blattidæ''; like a cockroach.

'''blaubok''', ''n.'' See ''blauwbok''.

'''blaud''' (blâd), ''n.''   [Sc., also ''blad'', perhaps same as ''blade'' (see ''blad''<sup>3</sup> and ''blade''); but cf. Gael. ''bladh'' = Ir. ''bladh'', a part.]   '''1.''' A large piece of anything; a considerable portion; a flat piece of anything.—'''2.''' A slap; a blow or stroke.

'''blaufish''' (blâ′fish), ''n.''   [< *''blau'', prob. same as Sc. ''bla'', ''blae'', dark, livid (see ''blae''), + ''fish''.]   According to Pennant, a name of the blackfish, ''Centrolophus pompilus''. See cut under ''Centrolophus''.

'''blaunch†''', ''a.'' An obsolete form of ''blanch''<sup>1</sup>.

'''blauwbok''' (blou′bok), ''n.''   [D., lit. blue buck, < ''blauw'' (''blaauw''), = E. ''blue'', + ''bok'' = E. ''buck''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' The Dutch colonial name of a South African antelope, ''Hippotragus'' (or ''Ægoceros'') ''leucophæus'', given on account of its bluish appearance, caused by the dark hide showing through light hair. {{smaller|It is related to the oryx, addax, etc., and has rather large horns curving backward. Also called ''blue''''}}{{smaller|buck, blue antelope,}}'' {{smaller|and}} ''{{smaller|etaac.}}''

'''2.''' A small South African antelope with very short straight horns and heavy hind quarters.

Also spelled ''blaubok.''

'''blaver, blavert''' (blā′vėr, -vėrt), ''n.'' Corrupt forms of ''blawort.'' [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Your gloves shall be o’ the green clover
Come lockerin’ to your hand,
Well dropper o’er wi’ blue ''blavers,''
That grow amang white land.</poem>
{{right|''Gardener Lad'' (Anon.).}}}}

'''blaw''' (blâ), ''v.''; pret. ''blew,'' pp. ''blawn,'' ppr. ''blawing.''   [Sc., = E. ''blow''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To blow; breathe; publish; brag; boast; magnify in narrative.—{{smaller|'''To blaw in one’s lug,''' to cajole; flatter a person. Hence, ''blaw-in-my-lug,'' a flatterer; a wheedler. Scott.}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To flatter; coax.

'''blawort''' (blā′wėrt), ''n.''   [Sc., also ''blavert, blaver'', q. v., < ''bla, blae'', blue, + ''wort''<sup>1</sup>: see ''blae'' and ''wort''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' The blue corn-flower; the bluebottle.—'''2.''' The round-leafed bell-flower.   ''Jamieson.''

'''blay'''<sup>1</sup> (blā), ''n.''   [Also written ''bley''; < ME. *''blaye'', *''bleye'', < AS. ''blǣge'' = D. ''blei'' = G. ''bleihe'', a blay.]   A local English name of the bleak.

'''blay'''<sup>2</sup>, ''a.'' and ''n.'' Same as ''blae''.

'''blayberry''', ''n.'' Same as ''blaeberry''.

'''blay-linen''', ''n.'' Same as ''blae-linen''.

'''blaze'''<sup>1</sup> (blāz), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''blase'' (Sc. ''bleeze'', earlier ''blese''); < ME. ''blase'', a flame, < AS. ''blæse'', ''blase'', a flame, torch, = MLG. LG. ''blas'' = MHG. ''blas'', a torch (cf. AS. ''blæst'', a flame); akin to ''blaze''<sup>3</sup>, q. v., but only remotely, if at all, to ''blaze''<sup>2</sup>, q. v. The AS. forms ''blysa, blysige'', a torch, etc., belong to another root: see ''blush''.]   '''1†.''' A torch; a fire-brand.—'''2.''' A flame; a flaming fire; a conflagration.
{{smaller block|To heaven the ''blaze'' uprolled. {{right|''Croly.''}}}}
{{smaller block|What heaps of books and pamphlets! now we shall have a glorious ''blaze''. {{right|''Hawthorne'', Old Manse, I.}}}}
'''3.''' Figuratively, brilliant sunlight; effulgence; brilliance: as, the ''blaze'' of day.
{{smaller block|As thy beautie hath made thee the ''blaze'' of Italy, so wil thy lightnesse make thee the bye word of the worlde. {{right|''Lyly'', Euphues, Anat. of Wit, p. 102.}}}}
{{smaller block|O, dark, dark, dark, amid the ''blaze'' of noon! {{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 80.}}}}
'''4.''' A sudden kindling up or bursting out, as of fire, passion, etc.; an active or violent display; wide diffusion.

{{smaller block|In his ''blaze'' of wrath. {{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., iv. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|The main ''blaze'' of it is past, but a small thing would make it flame again. {{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iv. 3.}}}}
'''5.''' In the game of poker, a hand (now seldom or never used) consisting of five court-cards, ranking between two pairs and three of a kind: so called in allusion to the blaze of color displayed.—'''In a blaze,''' {{smaller|on fire; in flames.}}—'''Like blazes,''' {{smaller|furiously; in or to an excessive degree. [Low.]}}
{{smaller block|The other little ones used to cry ''like blazes.'' {{right|''Mayhew.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The horse was so maddened by the wound, and the road so steep, that he went ''like blazes.'' {{right|''De Quincey'', Spanish Nun, p. 24.}}}}
'''The blazes,''' {{smaller|hell; perdition. Hence, ''to go to blazes,'' to go to perdition, or to the deuce. [Slang.]}}='''Syn. 2.''' {{smaller|''Glare,'' etc. See ''flame, n.''}}

'''blaze<sup>1</sup>''' (blāz), ''v.''; pret. ''blazed'', ppr. ''blazing.''   [Early mod. E. also ''blase'' (= Sc. ''bleeze, blese''); < ME. ''blasen'', blaze; from the noun.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To burst into flame; burn with a bright flame or fervent heat; flame: either literally or figuratively.
{{smaller block|Two red fires in both their faces ''blazed.'' {{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1353.}}}}
{{smaller block|Starry lamps and ''blazing'' cressets.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 728.}}}}
'''2.''' To send forth a bright light; shine like flame or fire: as, a ''blazing'' diamond.
{{smaller block|<poem>I lift mine eyes, and all the windows ''blaze''
With forms of saints and holy men who died.</poem>{{right|''Longfellow'', Sonnets on the Divina Commedia, iv.}}}}
{{smaller block|The cupola ''blazes'' with gigantic archangels, stationed in a ring beneath the supreme figure and face of Christ.
{{right|''J. A. Symonds'', Italy and Greece, p. 169.}}}}
'''3.''' To be conspicuous; shine brightly with the brilliancy of talents, heroic deeds, etc. [Poetic.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Mighty names
Have ''blazed'' upon the world and passed away.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Fifty Years.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To blaze away''', to fire away; keep on firing (with guns or artillery); work vigorously or with enthusiasm. See ''away'', 12.—'''To blaze out.''' (''a'') To throw out flame or light; shine forth. (''b'') To go out with a flare. (''c'') To break out with passion or excitement; speak or act violently.—'''To blaze up''', to burst into flame, and hence into passion, anger, etc.}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To set in a blaze. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Take him in and ''blaze'' the oak. {{right|''Hood.''}}}}
'''2.''' To temper (steel) by covering it while hot with tallow or oil, which is then burned off.—'''3.''' To cause to shine forth; exhibit vividly.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fiery eyes ''blaze'' forth her wrong.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 219.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>So spake the Father; and, unfolding bright
Toward the right hand his glory, on the Son
''Blazed'' forth unclouded deity.</poem>{{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 65.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To blaze out†''', to burn out; figuratively, exhaust in a blaze of passion or excess.}}

'''blaze<sup>2</sup>''' (blāz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''blazed'', ppr. ''blazing''.   [< ME. ''blasen'', blow, as a trumpet, < AS. *''blǣsan'', blow (= MD. ''blaesen'', D. ''blazen'', blow, sound a trumpet, = MLG. ''blasen'' = OHG. ''blāsan'', MHG. ''blāsen'', G. ''blasen'' = Icel. ''blāsa'' = Sw. ''blåsa'' = Dan. ''blæse'', blow, = Goth. ''blēsan'', in comp. ''ufblēsan'', puff up); prob., with formative ''-s'', from the root *''blā'' of ''blāwan'', blow, breathe: see ''blow''<sup>1</sup>, and cf. ''blast''.
